- GFR depends on net glomerular filtration pressure, surface area and permeability; urine output is additionally governed by hormonal water conservation and tubular handling.
- Oliguria during anaesthesia may be an appropriate response to AVP, low effective circulating volume and surgical stress, but can also indicate significant injury.
- Conversely non-oliguric AKI can be severe.
- The anaesthetist must assess circulating perfusion and damage mechanisms rather than treating any number of mL/h as an indication for automatic fluid loading.

- AKI can result from haemodynamic low-flow states, sepsis-associated microcirculatory/inflammatory injury, intrinsic renal disease and urinary obstruction.
- These categories overlap.
- The older ‘prerenal azotaemia → acute tubular necrosis’ sequence is useful conceptually but overly simplistic: injured tubules can coexist with preserved or increased total renal blood flow, and sepsis-associated AKI is influenced by cytokines, microvascular distribution, mitochondrial stress and altered cell energetics, not solely sustained global ischaemia.

## 6.2 Definition and staging: know the actual KDIGO criteria

The **KDIGO 2012 AKI definition** remains the established published framework in late 2026: increase in serum creatinine **≥26.5 µmol/L (0.3 mg/dL) in 48 h**, or **≥1.5 × baseline within the prior seven days**, or urine volume **<0.5 mL/kg/h for at least six hours**. Staging conveys severity and mortality risk but is not a treatment algorithm.

| **AKI stage** | **Creatinine criterion** | **Urine output criterion** |
|---|---|---|
| Stage 1 | 1.5–1.9 × baseline **or** ↑ ≥26.5 µmol/L | <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6–12 h |
| Stage 2 | 2.0–2.9 × baseline | <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥12 h |
| Stage 3 | ≥3 × baseline **or** creatinine ≥353.6 µmol/L with qualifying rise **or** initiation of KRT | <0.3 mL/kg/h for ≥24 h **or** anuria ≥12 h |

- Serum creatinine **lags behind actual GFR decline**, is influenced by muscle mass, fluid dilution, creatine supplementation and altered tubular secretion, and may understate injury in sarcopenic patients.
- After large-volume resuscitation, the creatinine concentration can fall from dilution even as true filtration deteriorates.
- Conversely acute changes in creatinine are not correctly interpreted by eGFR equations designed for steady-state kidney function.
- Record a credible pre-illness baseline, the timing of changes and fluid balance.
- The [KDIGO AKI/AKD guideline update page](https://kdigo.org/guidelines/acute-kidney-injury/) notes that a **2026 draft** has undergone public review, but do **not** present draft recommendations as final consensus while the update remains unpublished.

## 6.3 The patient with new oliguria in theatre: a disciplined diagnostic approach

- Oliguria is commonly taken as urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h over several hours, but a single low-output hour during surgery is not automatically AKI.
- First confirm measurement: is there an indwelling catheter, is it kinked or blocked, was the bladder emptied, and has output been omitted from the record?
- A bladder scan can distinguish retention from true low production.
- Examine the **time course** and accompanying changes in MAP, pulse pressure, blood loss, fluid balance, capnography, ventilator pressures, temperature and urine appearance.

- Then ask whether the patient is **underfilled**, **vasodilated**, **pump-failing**, **venously congested**, **intrinsically injured** or **obstructed**.
- A patient with severe right ventricular failure, high CVP, tense abdomen and oliguria may have excessive renal venous pressure; giving large fluid boluses may worsen filtration.
- Conversely the bleeding hypotensive patient with low preload and poor perfusion may benefit from prompt blood or balanced crystalloid.
- Vasopressors are frequently appropriate when vasodilation causes low effective renal perfusion, but they do not replace volume when there is true haemorrhage.

- Targeted investigations include repeat creatinine, K, bicarbonate/ABG, lactate, urinalysis with blood/protein and sediment when available, CK if rhabdomyolysis, inflammatory/infection tests, ultrasound for obstruction, and bedside echocardiography/volume assessment.
- Renal ultrasound is important with solitary kidney, hydronephrosis risk, urological surgery or unexplained obstruction, but a normal ultrasound does not exclude early obstruction or intrinsic pathology.
- Urinary sodium, fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) and FEUrea have important limits in sepsis, CKD, diuretics, contrast exposure and evolving tubular injury; low FENa does **not** prove the absence of tubular injury.

**Initial management must be cause-directed:**

- Stabilise airway and systemic perfusion, control bleeding, remove urinary obstruction, stop nephrotoxic exposures, adjust drug dosing and support volume status.
- If hypovolaemia is credible, give a reassessed test bolus rather than repeated unmeasured litres; if there is pulmonary oedema or elevated venous pressure, avoid fluid excess.
- After an appropriately resuscitated patient remains oliguric, a ‘furosemide challenge’ does not restore nephron function and should not substitute for evaluation.
- The furosemide stress test may be prognostic in selected specialised settings, but is not a cure for AKI.

## 6.4 AKI phenotypes: mechanisms change what you look for

**Haemodynamic/functional AKI.** Hypotension, low cardiac output, haemorrhage, vasodilation, high intrathoracic pressure and intra-abdominal hypertension reduce effective glomerular perfusion. Perfusion restoration may promptly improve GFR if tissue injury is limited. But structural damage can develop even without prolonged overt hypotension if renal reserve is low.

**Acute tubular injury:**

- Ischaemia, sepsis and nephrotoxins impair tubular epithelial transport and polarity, causing back-leak, obstruction by casts, inflammation and altered tubuloglomerular feedback.
- Muddy brown granular casts support tubular injury but are not required.
- Non-oliguric presentations occur.
- Creatinine and electrolyte abnormalities may persist after global perfusion has improved; careful supportive care is central while repair occurs.

**Glomerular/interstitial/vascular disease:**

- Haematuria with red-cell casts, significant proteinuria, eosinophilic drug exposure (though eosinophiluria is insensitive), systemic rash, pulmonary haemorrhage, hypertension or thrombotic microangiopathy should prompt early renal consultation.
- Distinguish acute glomerulonephritis, vasculitis, acute interstitial nephritis, TMA, renal embolism and renal vein thrombosis from simple ATN; a specific immunological or vascular treatment may be needed.

**Postrenal obstruction:**

- Prostatic enlargement, stones, pelvic tumour, clots, catheter occlusion and ureteric damage can cause rapid injury.
- Bilateral obstruction, obstruction of a solitary functioning kidney or bladder outlet obstruction are key scenarios.
- Relieve the obstruction urgently when associated with infection, AKI or severe electrolyte changes.
- Watch for post-obstructive diuresis and subsequent hypovolaemia/electrolyte depletion rather than assuming renal recovery is complete once urine starts flowing.

## 6.5 AKI prevention across the perioperative pathway

- Prevention begins with identification of **renal risk**, not a prophylactic infusion ordered in theatre.
- Important risk factors include pre-existing CKD, diabetes, advanced age, heart failure, vascular disease, anaemia, sepsis, major emergency surgery, prolonged procedures, major blood loss, nephrotoxic drugs, arterial cross-clamping and high-risk contrast exposure.
- A patient with CKD and severe hypertension may autoregulate at a higher pressure, so the same MAP that is tolerable in a healthy young adult may give inadequate renal perfusion to that individual.

**Preoperative:**

- Identify baseline creatinine/eGFR, urinary abnormalities, potassium, acid–base state, volume status and haemodynamic reserve.
- Review ACEi/ARB, diuretics, NSAIDs, SGLT2 drugs, metformin, antibiotics and recent contrast; decisions to omit or continue chronic drugs should be individualised and aligned with surgery and institutional protocols.
- Correct true dehydration, optimise heart failure/haemoglobin where possible and discuss high risk in consent.
- Consider whether a planned contrast study is necessary and whether hydration/contrast-dose reduction is possible.
- There is no convincing evidence that routine N-acetylcysteine or prophylactic bicarbonate prevents clinically meaningful contrast AKI.
- Avoid falsely equating every post-contrast creatinine rise with direct contrast causation because haemodynamic and disease factors confound association.

**Intraoperative:**

- Maintain perfusion and oxygen delivery, avoid major blood loss/anaemia and sustained hypotension, and achieve euvolaemia.
- The ADQI–POQI consensus recommends avoiding routine **restrictive/zero-balance** fluid strategies in major surgery, using goal-directed haemodynamic therapy in high-risk cases and maintaining **MAP >65 mmHg**, with potentially higher targets in chronic hypertension or other high-risk patients.
- MAP matters together with exposure **duration** and venous congestion.
- A patient with low MAP due to vasodilation may benefit more from noradrenaline than from another fluid litre; a patient with true haemorrhage needs prompt haemostatic resuscitation.
- Volatile versus TIVA choice is generally less important for kidney outcome than perfusion, oxygen delivery and avoiding preventable complications.
- No routine ‘renal-dose dopamine’, mannitol or forced diuresis should be prescribed for renal protection.

- Crystalloid evidence must be described without overstating it.
- Balanced solutions produce less hyperchloraemia than saline and are often favoured for large-volume perioperative resuscitation.
- However the Australasian [PLUS trial](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2114464) found **no difference** in 90-day mortality or major kidney outcomes between Plasma-Lyte 148 and saline in 5037 ICU patients.
- Thus ‘balanced is physiologically attractive’ is not synonymous with ‘every major RCT proves improved survival’.
- Avoid hydroxyethyl starch solutions in patients at kidney risk because of harm signals; albumin has selected indications but is not established as a universal renal-protective treatment.

**Postoperative:**

- Monitor urine output, kidney function and electrolytes, detect occult haemorrhage/sepsis, reduce preventable hypotension and hypoxaemia, treat significant venous congestion, and avoid avoidable nephrotoxins.
- Renal recovery and medication reconciliation require follow-up: an AKI episode increases future CKD and cardiovascular risk even if discharge creatinine improves.
- Arrange re-check of kidney function and albuminuria around **3 months** after AKI (earlier clinical monitoring as needed), and re-evaluate stopped renoprotective medication once stable rather than omitting indefinitely.

## 6.6 Specific perioperative hazards: vascular surgery, contrast and intra-abdominal pressure

- **Aortic cross-clamping** changes afterload, renal blood flow and distal perfusion.
- Suprarenal clamps directly interrupt renal perfusion, while infrarenal clamping can impair renal flow through altered renal vascular resistance, increased afterload, haemodynamic variation and inflammatory/ischemic consequences.
- During release, vasodilation, washout of metabolites and relative hypovolaemia can cause hypotension.
- Protect kidneys by planning the clamp level and time, avoiding sustained hypotension, preserving circulating volume, managing bleeding and reperfusion, limiting additional nephrotoxins and monitoring electrolytes/acidosis.
- There is no routine evidence-based pharmacological ‘renal protection cocktail’.

- For **EVAR**, risk depends on CKD, contrast volume, atheroembolism, renal artery involvement, intraoperative hypoperfusion, blood loss and complications.
- Coordinate limited necessary contrast, adequate hydration without overload, haemodynamic stability and follow-up creatinine.
- The 2014.2 ANZCA SAQ specifically tested AKI risk in EVAR and evaluation of renal preservation strategies; an answer should distinguish established perfusion/volume measures from poorly supported mannitol, dopamine or prophylactic bicarbonate.

- **Intra-abdominal hypertension/compartment syndrome** may reduce GFR by increasing renal venous and parenchymal pressure while compromising cardiac output.
- Sustained intra-abdominal pressure >20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction defines abdominal compartment syndrome in consensus usage; decompress or address the surgical cause when indicated, optimise abdominal compliance and avoid excessive fluid loading that aggravates visceral oedema.

**Practical renal-risk assessment and interpretation:**

- The most actionable early bedside signals are baseline kidney reserve (eGFR and albuminuria if known), exposure to sustained hypotension and blood loss, postoperative creatinine trend and urine output, and clinical evidence of sepsis, obstruction or venous congestion.
- A preserved urine output does not rule out injury.
- In a postoperative patient with oliguria and increasing CVP, hepatomegaly or RV dysfunction, evaluate venous congestion with focused ultrasonography and haemodynamics rather than giving repeated fluid challenges.
- In abdominal surgery, raised intra-abdominal pressure can directly impair renal filtration; assess bladder pressure when compartment syndrome is plausible.
- A stable creatinine after a large fluid load may reflect dilution rather than preserved kidney function.
- A documented follow-up plan after AKI should identify who repeats renal function and albuminuria and when chronic kidney-protective therapy will be reviewed.

## 6.7 What the major evidence establishes

- The ADQI–POQI perioperative AKI consensus supports a structured, risk-based plan rather than routine kidney-protective drugs.
- Large fluid trials show that differences in biochemical chloride effects do not necessarily translate into survival differences.
- Severe metabolic acidosis with AKI requires careful judgement about bicarbonate and kidney replacement therapy rather than an automatic pH target.
- In BICARICU-2 (2025), bicarbonate reduced KRT starts in severe acidemia with stage 2–3 AKI without improving 90-day survival.
- In contrast, SODa-BIC (2026) found no benefit in the 30-day composite of death, KRT or persistent renal dysfunction among a broader group of vasopressor-dependent patients with metabolic acidosis.
- The purpose of AKI prevention is adequate oxygen delivery, avoidance of kidney insults and early detection—not a particular urine output achieved with diuretics.

items.title: 7. Rhabdomyolysis: myocyte injury, pigment nephropathy and systemic complications
items.priority: P1 CORE (1 parent LO) + P3 MODERATE (2 parent LOs)
items.body:
## 7.1 Muscle cell destruction creates electrolyte and renal emergencies

- Rhabdomyolysis is skeletal muscle membrane injury releasing creatine kinase (CK), potassium, phosphate, myoglobin and other intracellular contents.
- Causes include crush injury, prolonged pressure/immobility, seizures, exertional heat illness, vascular limb ischaemia and reperfusion, malignant hyperthermia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, compartment syndrome, toxins (alcohol, cocaine, some medications), severe infection and metabolic myopathies.
- The classic triad of muscle pain, weakness and dark urine is **insensitive**; critical patients may present first with hyperkalaemia, acidosis or acute kidney injury.

- Myoglobin is freely filtered and can cause intrarenal vasoconstriction, oxidative tubular injury and pigment cast formation, particularly with volume depletion and acidic urine.
- Early hypovolaemia is common because fluid is sequestered into injured muscle.
- Potassium may rise abruptly and cause arrhythmia **before** creatinine becomes markedly abnormal; phosphorus rises, calcium may initially fall due to binding/deposition and later rebound hypercalcaemia can emerge during recovery.
- Limb compartment syndrome must be sought because unrelieved pressure continues muscle ischaemia; definitive treatment may require urgent fasciotomy.

## 7.2 Investigate the physiology and identify the precipitant

- CK >5 times the laboratory upper limit (often **>1000 U/L**) supports diagnosis, but its magnitude alone does not perfectly predict AKI or need for KRT.
- CK often peaks 24–72 h after injury.
- Serial creatinine, K, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate, urine output, ECG, lactate and haemoglobin are critical.
- Urine dipstick may show ‘blood’ with few or no red cells because myoglobin reacts with the haem pigment test; a negative urine myoglobin sample does not exclude rhabdomyolysis because myoglobin clears rapidly.
- Consider toxicology, vascular imaging, pressure injury evaluation, temperature and compartment-pressure/surgical assessment as clinically indicated.
- Check CK repeatedly in high-risk prolonged surgery, extreme lithotomy position, major crush or suspected malignant hyperthermia.

## 7.3 Treat perfusion failure, myonecrosis and hyperkalaemia—not CK in isolation

- Remove the precipitant, treat heat injury, stop offending drugs, control seizures, manage compartment syndrome and address vascular compromise.
- Early balanced crystalloid or another appropriate isotonic fluid can restore renal perfusion and urine flow in hypovolaemic patients, titrated to cardiac function and objective response.
- Published trauma consensus pathways sometimes cite **approximately 200–1000 mL/h** initially and urine output goals around **1–3 mL/kg/h (up to ≈300 mL/h)** in suitable adults, but these are resuscitation guides rather than a mandate to flood an anuric patient.
- Persistent oliguria despite corrected circulation should prompt assessment for established AKI and fluid accumulation.

- **Routine mannitol, forced diuresis or urinary alkalinisation is not supported** by robust evidence for preventing AKI compared with adequate volume resuscitation.
- Bicarbonate may be appropriate for significant systemic acidemia, but giving it solely to make urine alkaline can worsen sodium load, hypocalcaemia and volume status.
- Treat dangerous hyperkalaemia immediately with cardiac stabilisation and intracellular-shift therapy; KRT is indicated for refractory potassium, acidemia, pulmonary oedema or other conventional reasons, not solely because myoglobin or CK is high.
- Continuous KRT can remove some myoglobin depending on membrane and technique, but a serum CK threshold alone is not a KRT trigger.

## 7.4 Perioperative/risk scenarios worth anticipating

**Prolonged surgery or positioning:**

- Obesity, prolonged lateral/prone/lithotomy position, hypotension and external pressure may cause compression injuries; use appropriate padding, limit time where feasible and reassess severe postoperative muscle pain.
- **Trauma:** evaluate crush syndrome before releasing compression; anticipate sudden potassium release with reperfusion, prepare ECG, calcium, insulin/glucose and renal support.
- **Anaesthesia emergencies:** malignant hyperthermia and severe prolonged seizures can cause extensive muscle injury; treating the causal emergency (including dantrolene for MH as indicated) and monitoring kidney/metabolic sequelae are inseparable.

items.title: 8. Renal replacement therapy and anaesthesia for chronic kidney disease
items.priority: P1 CORE (1 parent LO) + P3 MODERATE (2 parent LOs) + P5 MINIMUM (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 8.1 Kidney replacement replaces functions, not kidney recovery

- Kidney replacement therapy (KRT; historically RRT) provides extracorporeal or peritoneal solute removal, acid–base/electrolyte correction and fluid removal while endogenous renal function is inadequate.
- It does **not reverse the primary injury**.
- The questions are: what dangerous problem cannot be controlled conservatively, which modality will achieve the goal safely, how much clearance is required and when can treatment stop?

The traditional teaching mnemonic **AEIOU** is useful but should not replace assessment:

- **A**cidosis that is severe and refractory despite causal management.
- **E**lectrolytes, particularly persistent dangerous hyperkalaemia.
- **I**ntoxications with dialysable toxins (e.g. lithium, ethylene glycol, methanol and selected cases of salicylate/metformin-associated lactic acidosis).
- Fluid **O**verload with hypoxaemia despite appropriate medical therapy.
- Symptomatic **U**raemia (pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding, refractory nausea).

- Other reasons include severe persisting electrolyte disturbances, fluid removal needed to allow nutrition/ventilation, and specific hypercatabolic states.
- Neither a single creatinine nor oliguria duration by itself proves an indication.

**Initiation timing evidence:**

- [STARRT-AKI (2020)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32668114/) randomised nearly 3000 critically ill patients with severe AKI to accelerated or standard initiation.
- Ninety-day mortality was virtually identical (**43.9% vs 43.7%**); accelerated initiation exposed more patients to KRT and increased dialysis dependence among survivors (10.4% vs 6.0%).
- The message is **do not start KRT purely because AKI is labelled severe before a genuine indication emerges**, provided close surveillance and rescue capability exist.
- Conversely waiting for arbitrary biochemical extremes in a patient with refractory hyperkalaemia, pulmonary oedema or uraemic complications would misapply the trial.
- AKIKI and IDEAL-ICU also inform the timing debate, and ELAIN differs in population/thresholds; integrate trial context rather than memorising ‘early is bad’ as a universal rule.

## 8.2 How solutes and water cross the filter

- There are three major physicochemical processes.
- **Diffusion** moves small solutes down a concentration gradient across a semipermeable membrane, driven by dialysate flowing in the opposite direction: particularly effective for urea, potassium and many small dialysable toxins.
- **Convection** uses transmembrane pressure to drag plasma water through the membrane, carrying dissolved solutes (‘solvent drag’) depending on molecule size and membrane sieving coefficient.
- **Ultrafiltration** is net removal of plasma water to manage volume; ultrafiltration can occur with both haemodialysis and haemofiltration, but convective solute clearance is specifically linked to large-volume replacement flow.
- **Adsorption** onto membrane or sorbent surfaces is a smaller additional mechanism relevant to certain specialized technologies.

- In intermittent haemodialysis, high dialysate and blood flows give rapid diffusion-based clearance, often over **3–4 hours**, with ultrafiltration as needed.
- This rapidly treats severe hyperkalaemia and selected intoxications but can cause hypotension and large osmotic shifts.
- In continuous techniques, blood flow is lower, clearance per minute is slower, but fluid and metabolic correction can be smooth over 24 hours—often preferable in vasopressor-dependent shock or raised intracranial pressure.
- Hybrid prolonged intermittent modalities (SLED/PIRRT) occupy the middle ground and can be practical when continuous machines are scarce.

| **Modality** | **Principal clearance** | **Practical advantage** | **Important limitation** |
|---|---|---|---|
| IHD (intermittent haemodialysis) | High-efficiency diffusion ± UF | Rapid K/toxin clearance; treatment-free intervals | Intradialytic hypotension and osmotic shifts |
| CVVH (continuous venovenous haemofiltration) | Convection via replacement fluid | Continuous fluid management; greater convective middle-solute component | Filter clotting, replacement fluid and predilution reduce effective clearance |
| CVVHD (continuous venovenous haemodialysis) | Diffusion via dialysate | Efficient continuous small-solute removal | Filter/circuit burden; may clear drugs significantly |
| CVVHDF | Both diffusion and convection | Flexible continuous small/middle-solute and fluid control | Prescription complexity; filter/circuit adverse effects |
| SLED/PIRRT | Mostly diffusion over prolonged session | Gentler than conventional IHD; no constant circuit | Clearances and stability depend on technique; may still cause hypotension |
| Peritoneal dialysis | Diffusion and osmosis across peritoneum | No vascular access; common chronic therapy | Less rapid emergency K clearance; unsuitable in some abdominal pathology |

- A typical extracorporeal pathway is **vascular access → blood pump → filter → return to patient**, with dialysate on the opposite side of the membrane for diffusion and replacement solution infused before/after the filter for convection; effluent exits to waste.
- **Predilution** reduces haemoconcentration and filter clotting but dilutes blood entering the membrane, reducing effective clearance for a given replacement volume.
- **Postdilution** improves clearance efficiency but may increase filtration fraction and haemoconcentration.
- Net patient fluid removal is distinct from effluent generated by dialysis/filtration and must be prescribed separately.

## 8.3 Prescription parameters worth understanding rather than memorising

**Access:**

- A large-bore dual-lumen temporary dialysis catheter is usually required for acute KRT, preferably in the right internal jugular vein when feasible; femoral access may be acceptable depending on anatomy and infection considerations.
- Avoid subclavian access in patients who may need long-term fistula because venous stenosis jeopardises future access.
- Review catheter tip position, securement, infection and recirculation.

**Blood flow:**

- Typical CRRT blood flows may be around **150–250 mL/min**, depending on circuit, catheter and patient.
- Poor flow promotes clotting and reduces delivered clearance.
- **Effluent dose** is dialysate plus ultrafiltration/replacement volumes (with modality-specific adjustments), conventionally normalised to weight as mL/kg/h.
- The established [KDIGO/KHA-CARI recommendation](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4056805/) for CRRT is **delivered 20–25 mL/kg/h**, usually necessitating prescription around 25–30 mL/kg/h to account for interruptions.
- The ANZ **RENAL trial (2009)** compared **40 vs 25 mL/kg/h prescribed** and found no mortality benefit from high-intensity therapy.
- Extremely catabolic states or rapid toxin clearance require individualized prescriptions, but increasing CRRT intensity is not an established routine survival intervention.

**Anticoagulation:**

- Regional citrate anticoagulation binds ionised calcium within the extracorporeal circuit and limits clotting without systemic anticoagulation when functioning correctly.
- Calcium must then be replaced systemically.
- Monitor **systemic and postfilter ionised calcium**, total calcium, acid–base and lactate.
- With inadequate citrate metabolism (severe shock, liver dysfunction), citrate may accumulate: rising total-to-ionised calcium ratio (often **>2.5**), worsening hypocalcaemia and acidosis are warning signals.
- Conversely efficient metabolism can cause alkalosis because citrate generates bicarbonate equivalents.
- Heparin is an alternative but adds systemic bleeding risk and possibility of HIT.
- Unanticoagulated circuits may be chosen in bleeding patients, accepting more frequent filter loss.
- Check drug/line compatibility; magnesium and phosphate can fall during CRRT and require surveillance.

**Net ultrafiltration:**

- Removing litres from an oedematous patient is not necessarily renal perfusion optimisation: if the plasma refill rate is inadequate, aggressive UF causes hypotension and additional kidney ischemia.
- Set removal in light of vasopressors, lactate, cardiac function, venous congestion, capillary leak and fluid intake; reassess frequently.
- Drug clearance can become unexpectedly high during CRRT, especially for small, low protein-bound drugs with modest volume of distribution, so antibiotic loading/maintenance and therapeutic drug monitoring matter.
- Hypothermia, nutrient/vitamin loss, electrolyte shifts and circuit access complications are also clinically relevant.

**Worked CRRT prescription for a 70-kg patient:**

- If the goal is a delivered clearance dose of 25 mL/kg/h, the patient needs roughly 1,750 mL/h effective effluent clearance.
- Prescribing around 2,000–2,100 mL/h may compensate for pauses and downtime, but the delivered dose must be calculated from actual treatment time and modality; predilution reduces solute clearance at a given nominal replacement flow.
- Separately prescribe a patient net fluid-removal target—for example a carefully titrated 0–100 mL/h during early vasopressor-dependent shock—and remember that replacement flow does not equal net removal.
- In CVVHDF, dialysate contributes diffusive clearance and replacement fluid convective clearance, so filter dose, patient fluid balance and regional anticoagulation are three distinct prescriptions.
- Audit the circuit’s actual running time, electrolytes, phosphate, magnesium, temperature, blood pressure and drug levels rather than assuming the machine’s displayed setpoints equal delivered treatment.

**Citrate anticoagulation: recognise both accumulation and overload:**

- Regional citrate chelates calcium before the filter to prevent clotting, while a separate systemic calcium infusion replaces calcium lost into effluent.
- Target postfilter and systemic ionised calcium using the local circuit protocol.
- Rising systemic calcium infusion requirement, worsening ionised hypocalcaemia, metabolic acidosis and a total-calcium/ionised-calcium ratio above about 2.5 suggest citrate accumulation; stop or reduce citrate and reassess circuit anticoagulation, shock and liver metabolism urgently.
- When citrate is metabolised efficiently but delivered in excess relative to clearance, metabolic alkalosis can develop.
- Liver failure raises risk, but it is not always an absolute citrate contraindication if local experience and intensive monitoring are available; the relevant question is current citrate clearance and haemodynamic/mitochondrial function.
- Heparin offers an alternative with systemic bleeding and HIT risks.

## 8.4 Choosing modality and stopping support

- In profound shock, severe brain injury or cerebral oedema, CRRT or carefully controlled PIRRT often limits abrupt osmotic and blood pressure shifts.
- IHD may be best for **immediately life-threatening hyperkalaemia or dialysable intoxication** where rapid removal is essential and haemodynamics permit.
- Some centres alternate modalities as the patient stabilises.
- Do not assume an inferior mortality outcome from one modality solely because continuous filtration looks physiologically gentler; robust trials have not demonstrated clear universal survival superiority.

- Assess recovery through a **rising spontaneous urine output, falling or stabilising creatinine off treatment, improved electrolyte/acid–base stability and ability to manage fluid balance without dialysis**.
- A diuretic-induced output does not directly show GFR recovery.
- Transition to intermittent support when vasopressors are minimal and fluid removal/solute needs can be managed safely.
- Avoid stopping KRT because creatinine looks low while the machine is actively clearing it.
- Discuss prognosis and goals of care when multiorgan failure is persistent.

## 8.5 Chronic kidney disease and dialysis: why anaesthesia risk is systemic

- Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is persistent kidney abnormality (typically **≥3 months**) defined by GFR and/or damage markers such as albuminuria.
- The distinction between CKD and AKI matters because anaemia, mineral-bone disorder and cardiovascular changes develop over time, while acute changes increase unpredictability.
- Stage G5 is eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73m²; patients with end-stage kidney disease may use haemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis or receive kidney transplantation.
- A ‘normal’ K on the morning of surgery does not exclude profound volume or cardiovascular derangement in a dialysis-dependent patient.

**Cardiovascular changes drive much of the risk:**

- Longstanding hypertension, LVH, coronary disease, impaired diastolic relaxation, arterial stiffness, calcific valvular disease, heart failure, pulmonary hypertension and autonomic dysfunction are common.
- Dialysis can cause myocardial stunning, hypotension and variable preload.
- Assess exertional capacity, angina, dyspnoea, orthopnoea, recent echocardiography where indicated, functional dialysis history and dry weight.
- CKD is associated with increased perioperative MACE, arrhythmia, infection and mortality.

- **Haematological/immune effects** include reduced erythropoietin and anaemia, iron deficiency, platelet dysfunction associated with uraemia, and impaired immune responses.
- Uraemic platelet dysfunction causes impaired platelet adhesion/aggregation even with a normal count; treat clinically relevant bleeding with dialysis optimisation, correction of anaemia and sometimes **desmopressin 0.3 µg/kg IV** for short-term effect under local protocol.
- The duration is short and repeat dosing may be limited by tachyphylaxis and hyponatraemia risk.
- Antiplatelet drugs and anticoagulation add further bleeding considerations.
- Dialysis patients may have chronic hepatitis or vascular access infection and should be assessed specifically.

- **Metabolic effects** include hyperkalaemia, acidosis, volume overload, hyperphosphataemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism and disturbed calcium/vitamin D.
- Drug pharmacokinetics change from altered renal clearance, protein binding and volume of distribution; metabolites of morphine and some other analgesics accumulate.
- **Atracurium/cisatracurium** undergo organ-independent Hofmann elimination (cisatracurium also ester hydrolysis), making them useful in severe renal dysfunction, while rocuronium duration may be prolonged and sugammadex–rocuronium complex clearance markedly reduced in severe renal failure.
- Although sugammadex can reverse blockade in haemodialysis patients, labelling, institutional policy and careful monitoring are relevant because of prolonged complex persistence; use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring and avoid unsupported claims of guaranteed rapid elimination.
- Suxamethonium may be used in renal failure when potassium is verified normal and no other contraindication exists, but hyperkalaemia and denervation concerns must be assessed.

## 8.6 Preoperative dialysis planning and intraoperative care

- **Before surgery**, determine dialysis modality, last treatment and next session, interdialytic weight gain, dry weight, access, recent complications, anticoagulation used during dialysis, BP variability and most recent K/Ca/Mg/phosphate/bicarbonate.
- Elective haemodialysis patients often benefit from dialysis on the **day before surgery** so volume and electrolytes are optimised without the immediate risk of post-dialysis hypovolaemia; if urgent dialysis is required on the day of surgery, coordinate heparin-free or modified anticoagulation when bleeding risk is high.
- Do not place BP cuffs, venepuncture or cannulae on a functioning or planned fistula arm.
- Peritoneal dialysis patients may require the abdomen drained before certain procedures; plan dialysate management and postoperative peritonitis prevention with nephrology.

- **Anaesthetic technique** may be general, regional or combined according to procedure, coagulation, vascular access and haemodynamics.
- Neuraxial approaches require review of uraemic platelet function, anticoagulants and recently administered dialysis heparin; an apparently normal INR/platelet count is not sufficient to dismiss dysfunction.
- Perform meticulous airway assessment if diabetic autonomic neuropathy or dialysis-associated gastroparesis/volume status alters risk.
- Avoid prolonged hypotension and overly liberal fluid loading.
- Anuric dialysis patients cannot excrete routine large volumes: administer fluids according to blood loss, actual intravascular need, cardiovascular reserve and dialysis plan.
- Monitor glucose carefully because reduced renal insulin metabolism may increase hypoglycaemia risk.

**Postoperative:**

- Monitor volume status, pulmonary oedema, hyperkalaemia, acidosis, bleeding, analgesic accumulation, dialysis access and need for early haemodialysis.
- Plan analgesia using paracetamol, regional techniques where appropriate and renal-adjusted opioid choices; avoid routine NSAIDs in significant CKD/AKI.
- Prevent fistula thrombosis by avoiding hypotension and compression.
- Consider serum K after transfusion, rhabdomyolysis or tissue injury.
- The follow-up plan should state dialysis timing and postoperative medication adjustments explicitly.

items.title: 9. Acute liver failure and acute-on-chronic liver failure
items.body:
## 9.1 The liver is a metabolic, synthetic and circulatory organ

- The workbook explicitly assigns **SS_IC 1.92: management of acute and acute-on-chronic liver failure, including transplantation**, to this set.
- Although it extends beyond the renal focus, it belongs naturally after acid–base, electrolyte and organ support because liver failure changes lactate clearance, gluconeogenesis, ammonia metabolism, coagulation, drug handling and intravascular homeostasis.
- A patient with liver failure can therefore develop hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, metabolic acidosis, vasodilatory shock, AKI and brain injury together.

- **Acute liver failure (ALF)** conventionally means new hepatic synthetic dysfunction with **INR ≥1.5 and hepatic encephalopathy**, generally within 26 weeks of illness, in someone without established cirrhosis (some conditions such as Wilson disease can complicate strict definitions).
- Do not call severe transaminitis alone ALF: hepatocellular injury can be impressive without loss of synthetic function.
- Conversely patients with very modest aminotransferases can have advanced failure after the initial injury peak.
- **Acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF)** is acute deterioration of chronic advanced liver disease accompanied by extrahepatic organ dysfunction and substantial short-term mortality; definitions vary by international consortium.
- The management emphasis is precipitant treatment, organ support and early discussion of transplantation eligibility.

## 9.2 Why the clinical consequences develop

- **Coagulopathy** reflects reduced hepatic synthesis of both procoagulant and natural anticoagulant proteins, together with thrombocytopenia, hyperfibrinolysis or fibrinogen changes depending on the cause.
- INR is a useful marker of synthetic failure and transplant prognosis but is **not a complete measure of bleeding risk**, particularly in cirrhosis where haemostasis may be ‘rebalanced’.
- Correct INR with plasma only for an actual bleeding/procedure indication when appropriate, not reflexively to normalise a number.
- Consider fibrinogen, platelet count and viscoelastic assays for procedural haemostasis.

- **Encephalopathy** reflects ammonia accumulation, neuroinflammation and altered astrocyte osmolar regulation.
- In ALF, rapidly rising ammonia may cause cerebral oedema and **intracranial hypertension**, especially with grade III–IV encephalopathy.
- Other contributors include hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, infection, sedatives and GI bleeding.
- Cerebral perfusion is threatened by hypotension and hyperventilation-induced cerebral vasoconstriction.
- In established chronic cirrhosis, encephalopathy is often precipitated by infection, constipation, GI bleed, dehydration or sedative exposure and is usually not identical to ALF cerebral oedema physiology.

**Circulation and kidneys:**

- Advanced liver failure can produce systemic and splanchnic vasodilation, effective arterial underfilling, activation of sympathetic/renin–angiotensin pathways, AVP release and renal vasoconstriction.
- This contributes to dilutional hyponatraemia and **hepatorenal syndrome–AKI**, a functional renal circulatory syndrome diagnosed after evaluating reversible causes and structural kidney injury.
- Sepsis, bleeding, nephrotoxins and intrinsic tubular injury remain common and can coexist.
- Do not assume every creatinine rise in cirrhosis is HRS.

**Metabolism:**

- Failure of hepatic gluconeogenesis/glycogen storage produces hypoglycaemia; reduced lactate clearance exacerbates hyperlactataemia; drug metabolism and protein binding change unpredictably.
- Inflammatory stress may cause respiratory alkalosis, whereas shock and AKI cause metabolic acidosis, creating characteristic mixed blood gases.
- Hypophosphataemia may occur during hepatic regeneration and phosphate should be monitored and replaced carefully if needed.

**Distinguishing acute liver failure from acute-on-chronic liver failure:**

- Classical adult ALF requires acute liver injury with coagulopathy (often INR ≥1.5) and hepatic encephalopathy in a patient without established cirrhosis, generally over an illness of less than 26 weeks.
- Severe acute liver injury without encephalopathy needs the same urgent causal evaluation and close observation but is not conventionally labelled ALF.
- ACLF instead develops in a patient with advanced chronic liver disease and superimposed deterioration, often triggered by infection, gastrointestinal bleeding, alcohol-related hepatitis, drug injury or surgery, with one or more extrahepatic failures.
- Prognosis is strongly determined by kidney, circulatory, respiratory and cerebral failure as well as the liver tests.
- EASL-CLIF and APASL approaches have historically used different entry criteria, so specify the system when quoting an ACLF grade.
- A late-2026 global multisociety consensus provides a newly harmonised definition and explicitly weights extrahepatic organ dysfunction/failure; older ACLF scoring systems should not be presented as identical to that framework.

## 9.3 Find the cause because several causes have disease-specific treatment

- Urgent history focuses on paracetamol ingestion (including repeated supra-therapeutic dosing), prescription and herbal drugs, viral exposures, autoimmune disease, pregnancy (acute fatty liver/HELLP), ischaemia/shock, Wilson disease, Budd–Chiari syndrome and mushroom poisoning.
- Order repeated INR/PT, AST/ALT, bilirubin, albumin, glucose, lactate, blood gas, U&E, creatinine, calcium/phosphate/Mg, FBC, cultures, hepatitis testing, autoimmune tests and paracetamol concentration; assess pregnancy and drug/toxicology tests where indicated.
- Doppler liver imaging evaluates vascular patency and biliary disease.
- Lactate, ammonia and mental status are prognostically important but require careful interpretation.

- A very high AST/ALT (thousands) with relatively early low bilirubin suggests paracetamol or ischaemic injury among other causes; severe Wilson-associated ALF may show striking bilirubin with comparatively low ALP and haemolysis.
- Imaging may appear nodular after massive hepatic necrosis without established pre-existing cirrhosis.
- **Early discussion with a transplant centre is essential**; do not wait until the patient meets every prognostic criterion, because transfer may become unsafe once cerebral oedema, shock or renal failure develop.

## 9.4 Initial and intensive care management

**A/B/C and monitoring:**

- Protect the airway with grade III–IV encephalopathy, failure to protect airway, seizures or progressive cerebral oedema; use controlled induction mindful of profound vasodilation, aspiration risk and potential raised ICP.
- Avoid hypoxaemia, prolonged hypotension, fever and large rapid sodium changes.
- Monitor arterial pressure, glucose (often hourly if unstable), electrolytes/acid–base, INR, lactate, ammonia and renal function frequently; use early ICU and hepatology/transplant teams.
- Treat infection promptly and consider diagnostic paracentesis in decompensated cirrhosis with ascites to exclude spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

**Specific therapy:**

- Give **N-acetylcysteine (NAC)** promptly for suspected or confirmed paracetamol toxicity and consider it early in selected non-paracetamol ALF, recognising that evidence is stronger for improved transplant-free survival in earlier-stage non-paracetamol encephalopathy than in very advanced disease.
- Dose and duration must follow local toxicology/paracetamol protocols, which differ internationally and may be adjusted for massive ingestion.
- Consider **aciclovir** if HSV hepatitis is plausible
- Antivirals for HBV-related ALF
- Directed treatment for autoimmune hepatitis in selected patients
- Expedited obstetric delivery for pregnancy-specific disease as indicated
- Reperfusion/haemodynamic treatment for ischaemic hepatitis
- And toxin-specific management.
- Avoid hepatotoxic drugs and titrate potentially sedating medications carefully.

**Cerebral protection:**

- Assess encephalopathy serially, avoid hyponatraemia and fever, elevate head and maintain cerebral perfusion.
- Hypertonic saline may be used in high-risk cerebral oedema or intracranial hypertension with specialist targets; mannitol is a possible rescue therapy if haemodynamics/kidney function permit.
- Do not prophylactically hyperventilate to low PaCO₂; transient rescue hyperventilation may be considered for impending herniation while definitive treatment occurs.
- Ammonia is cleared by KRT, sometimes using continuous techniques in severe ALF with hyperammonaemia even before conventional uraemic indications, in consultation with transplant/neurocritical teams.
- Seizure control and sedative choice must balance neuro-observation against airway safety.

**Circulation/renal support:**

- Restore effective volume cautiously using measured responsiveness, then vasopressors—often noradrenaline—for vasodilatory shock; prevent venous congestion and pulmonary oedema.
- Diagnose AKI systematically.
- In suspected HRS-AKI with cirrhosis, treat precipitants, stop diuretics/nephrotoxins when appropriate, consider **albumin plus vasoconstrictor therapy** according to current specialist protocols (e.g. terlipressin in suitable patients, with special caution in hypoxaemia/respiratory failure).
- Severe ALF/ACLF may require CRRT to correct acidosis, potassium, fluid overload and ammonia burden while preserving haemodynamic and cerebral stability.

**Coagulation and bleeding:**

- Use clinical bleeding status, procedure type, platelet count/fibrinogen and viscoelastic methods to decide on component therapy.
- Prophylactic plasma can obscure INR trends used in transplant prognostication and causes overload; do not transfuse it solely for INR.
- Stress-ulcer measures, targeted GI bleed management, infection prevention and appropriate thrombosis prophylaxis are still relevant—liver disease does not eliminate VTE risk.
- Nutritional support and micronutrient replacement, including glucose and phosphate, are integral rather than optional extras.

**Hepatorenal syndrome–AKI: current diagnostic pathway:**

- In cirrhosis with ascites and AKI by KDIGO creatinine and/or urine criteria, assess intravascular volume, sepsis, bleeding, nephrotoxins, obstruction and structural renal disease.
- The 2024 ADQI–International Club of Ascites consensus permits HRS-AKI diagnosis if kidney function does not improve within 24 hours of adequate resuscitation when clinically indicated and there is no strong alternative primary cause; it specifically recommends against a mandatory 48-hour albumin challenge.
- Do not give indiscriminate albumin to an overloaded or hypoxaemic patient just to satisfy an older diagnostic rule.
- Once HRS-AKI is established, specialist therapy commonly combines a vasoconstrictor (terlipressin where suitable) with carefully titrated 20–25% albumin.
- Assess oxygenation and fluid status throughout: terlipressin can precipitate or worsen respiratory failure, and the syndrome may coexist with tubular injury.
- Transplant assessment and source-control treatment of precipitants run in parallel with renal support decisions.

## 9.5 Transplantation, prognosis and treatment limitation decisions

- **King’s College criteria** support urgent transplant referral but are imperfect and do not replace clinical judgement.
- For **paracetamol-related ALF**, the classic criteria are arterial **pH <7.3 after resuscitation**, or all of **INR >6.5**, creatinine **>300 µmol/L** and grade III–IV encephalopathy.
- For **non-paracetamol ALF**, classic criteria include **INR >6.5** irrespective of encephalopathy, or combinations of age extremes, high bilirubin, prolonged jaundice-to-encephalopathy interval, high INR and unfavourable aetiology.
- Different published versions use slightly different boundaries and transplant units apply updated local approaches including lactate, trajectory, cause and organ-support needs.
- The [Transplantation Society of Australia and New Zealand criteria](https://tsanz.com.au/) and [AASLD ALF guidance](https://www.aasld.org/practice-guidelines/management-acute-liver-failure) should anchor discussions, not operate as rigid boxes to tick.

- For **ACLF**, assess reversible precipitants, extrahepatic organ failures, baseline liver disease, frailty, alcohol/substance history in a non-stigmatising clinically relevant way, and transplant suitability.
- Scores such as MELD(-Na) and organ-failure-based systems inform prognosis but cannot replace a multidisciplinary conversation.
- The **2017 ANZCA Blue Book chapter “Anaesthesia for patients with liver disease”** and **2023 chapter “Perioperative considerations for the patient with portal hypertension”** provide practical regional context for perioperative assessment and procedures; contemporary ALF-specific management additionally requires transplant and critical-care guidance.

## 9.6 Anaesthesia in a patient with liver failure

**Preoperative:**

- Determine whether disease is acute versus chronic, severity of encephalopathy, aspiration risk, functional status, coagulopathy/platelets, volume status, ascites, renal injury, glucose, sodium, acid–base, infection, cardiopulmonary disease, portal hypertension and reasons for the procedure.
- The clinical question is whether proceeding provides urgent source control or transplant benefit versus an avoidable physiologic insult.
- Time-critical interventions may need to proceed despite severe organ dysfunction with ICU support.

**Intraoperative:**

- Use invasive monitoring in unstable/high-risk procedures; protect cerebral and renal perfusion, avoid unnecessary chloride and hypotonic loads, correct severe glucose/electrolyte disturbances, titrate sedatives/opioids to altered protein binding/clearance and be ready for severe haemodynamic instability.
- Positive pressure and PEEP must balance oxygenation with venous return in vasodilated or RV-compromised patients.
- Neuraxial techniques require a careful haemostatic risk assessment, not just a superficial INR cut-off.
- Consider varices/upper GI bleeding risk when choosing gastric instrumentation and TEE.

**Postoperative:**

- Anticipate encephalopathy, delayed drug elimination, bleeding, renal worsening, pulmonary oedema and glucose disturbances.
- Continue early frequent laboratory testing and neurology/circulatory surveillance; coordinate transplant or hepatology decisions and goals of care.
- An apparently acceptable early postoperative course does not mean the patient is metabolically stable.

items.body:
- The examination tests clinical judgement rather than the ability to recognise an isolated laboratory value.
- These cases demonstrate how the preceding physiology leads to a decision about timing of surgery, resuscitation, ventilation, dialysis and postoperative disposition.
- The numbers are illustrative; clinical management must use laboratory-specific reference ranges and current local protocols.

## 10.1 The patient with a severe mixed acidosis before emergency surgery

- A 68-year-old patient with perforated viscus and septic shock requires immediate laparotomy.
- Noradrenaline is running, lactate is 9 mmol/L, pH 7.12, PaCO₂ 32 mmHg and bicarbonate 10 mmol/L; sodium is 139, chloride 104, albumin 20 g/L.
- The **primary disorder is metabolic acidosis**.
- The measured anion gap is 139 − (104 + 10) = **25 mmol/L**; correcting for albumin of 20 g/L gives approximately **30 mmol/L**, strongly supporting unmeasured anions such as lactate.
- Winter’s predicted PaCO₂ is (1.5 × 10) + 8 = **23 ± 2 mmHg**.
- The actual PaCO₂ of 32 mmHg is inadequately low for the severity of metabolic acidosis: **a simultaneous respiratory acidosis** is present, even though 32 mmHg would be labelled ‘low’ in isolation.
- Potential explanations include exhaustion, dead-space physiology, lung injury, inadequate ventilation or opioid effect.

- The intervention is not to chase a normal pH before life-saving surgery.
- **Restore oxygen delivery and achieve source control** while resuscitating the circulation; diagnose cardiopulmonary contributors to dead space and hypoventilation.
- Prepare for intubation-induced collapse: pre-induction vasopressor support, haemodynamic monitoring, treatment of relevant electrolyte abnormalities and a ventilation plan that prevents the abrupt fall in compensatory minute ventilation.
- After induction, reassess PaCO₂ promptly rather than assuming a conventional ventilator respiratory rate is sufficient.
- Consider bicarbonate only for a specific severe-acidaemia indication in the context of the evidence discussed in Chapter 2 and possible AKI, not as definitive therapy for ongoing tissue hypoperfusion.
- This also illustrates why blood gas trends and improving lactate/perfusion often matter more than the first post-induction pH.

## 10.2 A dialysis patient scheduled for surgery with potassium 6.0 mmol/L

- A patient on maintenance haemodialysis arrives fasting for major lower-limb revascularisation with potassium 6.0 mmol/L, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L and new breathlessness.
- These results cannot safely be interpreted as one uncomplicated ‘renal potassium problem’.
- Obtain an ECG immediately, repeat a non-haemolysed potassium, evaluate glucose and blood-gas pH, assess volume clinically and with focused ultrasound if useful, establish the timing and completion of the most recent dialysis session, check residual renal function and review RAAS blockade, trimethoprim and other contributors.
- Breathlessness may indicate pulmonary oedema, acute coronary syndrome, PE or another process; it is not necessarily uraemia.

- If ECG abnormalities or electrical instability are present, give **IV calcium immediately** and then shift potassium into cells with **insulin/glucose** (plus inhaled salbutamol as appropriate), while seeking definitive potassium removal, usually urgent haemodialysis.
- Even with a nondiagnostic ECG, persistent severe hyperkalaemia and impending anaesthesia require specialist discussion and active correction, not reassurance.
- The surgery’s urgency determines whether renal optimisation can occur first.
- When urgent surgery cannot wait, avoid succinylcholine in established significant hyperkalaemia, prepare vasopressors and calcium/glucose/insulin, carefully choose crystalloid and volume, monitor ECG and serial electrolytes, and plan postoperative dialysis and monitoring.
- Dialysis after recent intravascular fluid removal can also make induction hypotension unusually pronounced.

## 10.3 Polyuria during craniotomy: water diuresis is not automatically diabetes insipidus

- A patient undergoing suprasellar tumour surgery develops urine output of 650 mL over one hour.
- The differential begins with **mannitol**, hypertonic saline, hyperglycaemic osmotic diuresis, perioperative high-volume fluid administration, diuretic exposure and solute diuresis from urea, before concluding central arginine vasopressin (AVP) deficiency.
- Check serum sodium and glucose; paired serum and urine osmolality and urine specific gravity can distinguish a dilute water diuresis from osmotically concentrated urine.
- Consider recent endocrine history and surgical manipulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.
- A rising sodium, high serum osmolality and inappropriately dilute urine in a patient with large ongoing losses strongly suggest AVP deficiency.

- Replace haemodynamic deficits using appropriate crystalloid; then address the **electrolyte-free water deficit** and ongoing water losses without precipitating rapid sodium swings.
- Give carefully titrated desmopressin if AVP deficiency is confirmed and clinically significant, and perform close urine-output, sodium and fluid-balance monitoring: a dose that is excessive or given during a resolving transient postoperative phase can cause dangerous water retention and hyponatraemia.
- Anticipate a possible **triphasic** postoperative AVP response after pituitary surgery.
- This example aligns with the 2025.1 ANZCA SAQ on intraoperative AVP deficiency but is presented here as a physiologic teaching example, not a reconstructed official model answer.

## 10.4 Hypotension, hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia after steroid interruption

- A patient treated with chronic glucocorticoids has vomiting, abdominal pain, glucose 2.8 mmol/L, sodium 124 mmol/L and vasopressor-resistant shock after emergency surgery.
- This combination should raise immediate concern for **adrenal crisis**, although sepsis, bleeding, medication error and other shock causes must be pursued in parallel.
- If blood can be sampled without delaying treatment, measure cortisol/ACTH, but do not postpone therapy for a laboratory result.
- Give **hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately**, then **200 mg/24 h** by infusion or 50 mg every six hours, alongside isotonic fluid, dextrose for hypoglycaemia and treatment of any precipitant.
- Monitor potassium and glucose.
- Mineralocorticoid deficiency may contribute to hyperkalaemia in primary adrenal insufficiency, whereas isolated secondary adrenal insufficiency usually retains aldosterone.
- The haemodynamic response is not always instantaneous, and cortisol deficiency may coexist with infectious shock.

## 10.5 Oliguria with rising lactate after major vascular surgery

- Following prolonged suprarenal aortic clamping, urine output is 10 mL/hour and the patient is vasopressor-dependent.
- Reduced renal perfusion and ischaemia–reperfusion may be central, but first identify reversible causes of inadequate monitoring or drainage (blocked catheter), haemorrhage, low cardiac output, excessive vasoconstriction, abdominal compartment physiology and venous congestion.
- Urine output alone cannot establish ‘prerenal’ versus ‘intrinsic’ AKI.
- Assess perfusion pressure, pulse pressure/stroke-volume responsiveness where valid, echo function, lactate trend, volume balance and abdominal pressure if indicated.
- Avoid reflex litre-after-litre boluses: excessive venous pressure reduces effective renal filtration pressure and may worsen pulmonary and bowel oedema.
- Treat ongoing bleeding, restore adequate cardiac output and pressure, evaluate renal perfusion and follow serial creatinine/electrolytes/acid-base.
- Persistent oliguria with hyperkalaemia, refractory metabolic acidosis or pulmonary oedema may require KRT, but isolated oliguria is not itself an automatic dialysis trigger.

## 10.6 When the initial result and the trend disagree

- A shocked patient has a lactate of 8 mmol/L initially, falling to 3 after source control, but the base excess remains markedly negative after several litres of 0.9% saline.
- Chloride has increased from 100 to 115 mmol/L.
- This pattern can reflect **improved tissue oxygen delivery with persistent hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis** rather than treatment failure.
- Calculate the anion gap with albumin correction, inspect the chloride trend and correlate with perfusion and clinical state.
- Conversely, lactate may remain elevated because of impaired hepatic clearance or beta-agonist stimulation; normalising lactate does not guarantee adequate microvascular oxygenation in every organ.
- Decisions must integrate all available physiology.

items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
- **1.** **BICARICU-2 (2025).** Sodium bicarbonate for severe metabolic acidemia and AKI. JAMA. [Primary trial](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2025.20231). Useful for deciding whether correction of severe acidemia improves patient-centred outcomes rather than a surrogate pH.
- **2.** **SODa-BIC (2026).** Sodium bicarbonate for critically ill adults with metabolic acidosis and shock. N Engl J Med 395:1062–1074. Double-blind RCT (n=500); no improvement in MAKE30 with a bicarbonate infusion. [Read original trial (DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2600526)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2600526)
- **3.** Kitisin et al.
  - (2026).
  - Sodium bicarbonate therapy for metabolic acidosis in critically ill patients: a Bayesian systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
  - Intensive Care Medicine.
  - Four trials (n=1544): no clear short-term mortality benefit, possible reduction in RRT starts. [Read systematic review](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00134-026-08602-3)
- **4.** **PLUS (2022).** Balanced multielectrolyte solution versus saline in critically ill adults. NEJM. [Primary trial](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2114464). Interprets the clinical significance of chloride loading and fluid choice.
- **5.** **STARRT-AKI (2020).** Timing of initiation of renal-replacement therapy in AKI. NEJM. [Primary trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32668114/). Supports KRT initiation guided by urgent indications and close monitoring.
- **6.** **RENAL (2009).** Intensity of continuous renal-replacement therapy in the critically ill. NEJM. [Primary trial](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa0902413). Compares intensity prescriptions rather than modalities.
- **7.** **Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes (2024).** ADA/EASD/JBDS et al. [International consensus report](https://doi.org/10.2337/dci24-0032). Use for DKA/HHS diagnostic criteria, fluids, insulin and potassium safety.
- **8.** **Joint consensus statement on thyroid storm (2026).** [European Thyroid Journal](https://doi.org/10.1530/ETJ-26-0043). Contemporary thyroid-storm recognition and multi-pronged treatment.
- **9.** **ADQI–POQI perioperative AKI consensus (2021).** [Nature Reviews Nephrology](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41581-021-00418-2). Risk assessment, haemodynamic optimisation and kidney protection.

items.title: Reading list and linked references
items.body:
## Evidence audit and interpretation

The chapters were independently organised from the curriculum outcomes, then checked against the available ANZCA examination reports, relevant BJA Education reviews, ANZCA Blue Book chapters, official guidelines and primary trial publications. Clinical decisions are not treated as though every recommendation has equally strong trial evidence:

| **Topic** | **High-value evidence and the precise lesson for practice** |
|---|---|
| **Acid–base interpretation** | BJA Education 2022/2024 and MJA’s structured interpretation paper support a disciplined acid–base sequence; compensation equations are diagnostic aids, not treatment targets. |
| **Severe metabolic acidaemia in AKI** | **BICARICU-2 (2025):** bicarbonate in a specific severe-acidaemia/AKI population reduced exposure to KRT without a demonstrated 90-day mortality reduction; do not extrapolate to all lactic acidosis. |
| **Crystalloid composition and AKI** | **PLUS (2022)** found no significant 90-day mortality difference with balanced crystalloid versus saline in a broad ICU population. This does not negate chloride physiology or justify excessive chloride loading. |
| **DKA/HHS** | The **2024 international consensus** uses contemporary beta-hydroxybutyrate, pH/bicarbonate, glucose and osmolality criteria and risk-adapted fluid/insulin/potassium treatment. It supersedes several older diagnostic cut-offs. |
| **Endocrine emergencies** | **2026 joint thyroid-storm consensus** supports a coordinated multi-mechanism approach. Guidelines remain more decisive than trials for most crisis drug combinations because high-quality randomised evidence is limited. |
| **Hyperkalaemia** | **ANZCOR 2026** and an Australian Prescriber 2026 review distinguish myocardial stabilisation, temporary intracellular shift and actual potassium removal; no ECG sign reliably excludes danger. |
| **Perioperative AKI** | **ADQI/POQI (2021)** supports multimodal kidney protection and individualised haemodynamic/medication planning; no single ‘renal-dose’ drug reliably prevents AKI. |
| **Timing of KRT** | **STARRT-AKI (2020):** accelerated KRT without conventional urgent indications did not reduce mortality and increased dialysis dependence in survivors. Monitor for indications rather than starting by creatinine threshold alone. |
| **KRT intensity** | **RENAL (2009):** higher-intensity CRRT did not improve survival relative to 25 mL/kg/h prescription; achieving usual delivered targets reliably matters more than maximal effluent. |
| **Liver failure** | **AASLD** and current transplant-service guidance support aetiology-specific rescue therapy, organ support and early referral. Transplant prognostic criteria are aids, not substitutes for real-time transplant evaluation. |

2026 evidence-update findings. The independent audit confirmed the 2024 DKA/HHS diagnostic and potassium treatment thresholds, ANZCOR 2026 hyperkalaemic-arrest calcium/insulin/bicarbonate doses, the absence of a 90-day mortality benefit in BICARICU-2, and the neutral 30-day MAKE outcome in SODa-BIC (2026). It identified clinical-depth gaps in mixed acid–base interpretation, glucose targets, sodium overcorrection, perioperative SGLT2-associated DKA, CRRT prescription and HRS-AKI; these have been integrated above. The 2024 ADQI/ICA HRS-AKI update and a newly published 2026 global ACLF consensus are included with explicit separation between historical diagnostic criteria and more recent proposals. The 2022 BJA Education reference titles are also corrected below, and the 2023 mixed acid–base article has been added. A 2 November 2026 Bayesian trial meta-analysis is now included to distinguish possible reduction in RRT use from unproven survival benefit.

### Contextual ANZCA examiner signals

The workbook links this set to past questions involving the blood gas in shock, utility of VBG, hyperkalaemia during major burns, preoperative renal dysfunction with potassium 6.0 mmol/L, intraoperative AVP deficiency, severe hypomagnesaemia, renal protection during EVAR/aortic surgery and perioperative severe thyrotoxicosis. The clinical examples throughout the chapters were selected to strengthen the reasoning tested by these themes. **This is not a substitute for the separate Retrieve/SAQ/Speak documents:** past SAQs require their own examiner-report-grounded model answers and self-marking schedules.

### Source integrity and updating notes

- The currently available public **KDIGO AKI guideline is the 2012 published guideline**, with later consensus and review updates; a 2026 public-review draft should not be described as an adopted final guideline. The practical KDIGO diagnosis/staging criteria remain the basis used here.

- Hyperkalaemia thresholds and recommended doses can differ between resuscitation and nephrology pathways. Adult emergency doses are provided for examination learning; bedside treatment follows institutional protocols, monitoring and specialist input.

- Hypertonic saline, IV insulin, concentrated electrolytes, vasopressors, desmopressin and KRT prescriptions require pump, concentration, renal function and point-of-care verification. Sodium correction limits, in particular, are **safety ceilings**, not targets to reach.

- Blue Book articles are used to deepen contextual Australian/New Zealand perioperative application rather than replace disease-specific ICU consensus or trial evidence. Only relevant identifiable Blue Book chapters are attributed; no exhaustive Blue Book search or proprietary textbook verification is claimed.

### BJA Education and interpretive reviews

- **1.** **Acid–base balance: a review of normal physiology (2022).** BJA Education. [Read](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2022.06.003). Bicarbonate buffering, respiratory/renal compensation and normal variation.
- **2.** **Acid–base quantification: a review of developing technology (2022).** BJA Education. [Read](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2022.07.006). Anion gap, albumin correction and physicochemical reasoning.
- **3.** **Metabolic acidosis in anaesthesia and critical care (2024).** BJA Education. [Read](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.12.005). Clinical aetiology and perioperative risk.
- **4.** **A structured approach to acid–base interpretation (2019).** Medical Journal of Australia. [Read](https://www.mja.com.au/journal/2019/211/7/structured-approach-acid-base-interpretation). Worked multistep diagnostic framework.
- Park and Sidebotham (2023). Metabolic alkalosis and mixed acid–base disturbance in anaesthesia and critical care. BJA Education 23:128–135. Particularly useful for chloride/volume depletion and mixed metabolic disorders. [Read source](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.01.002)
- Shaw and Gregory (2022). Acid–base balance: a review of normal physiology. The published corrigendum corrects the Henderson–Hasselbalch equations. [Original article](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2022.06.003) | [Corrigendum](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2022.11.004%29)
- Shaw and Magee (2022). Acid–base quantification: a review of developing technology. [Read source](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2022.07.006)
- ADQI–International Club of Ascites consensus (2024). Hepatorenal syndrome–AKI diagnosis and treatment, including updated volume assessment and omission of mandatory albumin challenge. [Read source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11193657/)
- Global multisociety consensus on acute-on-chronic liver failure (2026). Newly published definitions and extrahepatic organ-failure grading; interpret alongside the historical EASL–CLIF framework. [Read source](https://www.journal-of-hepatology.eu/article/S0168-8278%2826%2902898-9/fulltext)
- ADA Standards of Care (2026), Diabetes Care in the Hospital. Perioperative SGLT2 interruption and ICU glycaemic targets. [Read source](https://diabetesjournals.org/care/article/49/Supplement_1/S339/163925/16-Diabetes-Care-in-the-Hospital-Standards-of-Care)
- Hyponatraemia treatment standard (2024), Nephrology Dialysis Transplantation. Hypertonic bolus and prevention of sodium overcorrection. [Read source](https://doi.org/10.1093/ndt/gfae162)
- Endocrine Society guideline (2023), Hypercalcaemia of malignancy. Clinical thresholds, calcitonin and antiresorptive therapies. [Read source](https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines/hypercalcemia)
- Society for Endocrinology inpatient guidance, central diabetes insipidus/AVP deficiency. Desmopressin and fluid/sodium monitoring. [Read source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6013691/)
- NICE-SUGAR Investigators (2009). Intensive versus conventional glucose control in critically ill patients. NEJM. Evidence for avoiding excessively tight ICU glycaemic targets. [Read trial](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa0810625)

### Clinical guidance and Australasian context

- **1.** **ANZCOR Guideline 11.10: Resuscitation in special circumstances (updated 2026).** [Guideline](https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-10-resuscitation-in-special-circumstances). Emergency potassium and related arrest scenarios.
- **2.** **Management of acute hyperkalaemia: evidence, practice and pitfalls (2026).** Australian Prescriber. [Read](https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/management-of-acute-hyperkalaemia-evidence-practice-and-pitfalls.html). Calcium, insulin/glucose, shift and removal safety.
- **3.** **Management of adrenal crisis (Society for Endocrinology).** [Guideline](https://www.endocrinology.org/clinical-practice/clinical-guidance/adrenal-crisis/). Adult emergency hydrocortisone and fluids.
- **4.** **KDIGO: Acute Kidney Injury.** [Official guideline portal](https://kdigo.org/guidelines/acute-kidney-injury/). Diagnostic criteria and evidence updates; distinguish published guidance from draft revisions.
- **5.** **Hyponatraemia: diagnosis and treatment (2024).** Nephrology Dialysis Transplantation. [Review](https://academic.oup.com/ndt/article/39/10/1583/7713921). Hypertonic saline boluses, ongoing monitoring and avoidance of overcorrection.
- **6.** **AASLD: Management of acute liver failure.** [Guidance](https://www.aasld.org/practice-guidelines/management-acute-liver-failure). Evaluation, treatment and transplant referral.
- **7.** **Transplantation Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ).** [2026 clinical guidelines](https://tsanz.com.au/storage/Guidelines/TSANZ_Clinical_Guidelines_Version-116_260420_final.pdf). Local transplantation assessment and indications; centres retain case-specific discretion.
- **8.** **ANZCA Australasian Anaesthesia (Blue Book) collection.** [Official collection](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29). Relevant focused reading: 2025 “The emergency laparotomy patient” (volume and perfusion risk), 2023 “100 years of insulin” (insulin history/context), 2023 “Perioperative considerations for the patient with portal hypertension”, and 2017 “Anaesthesia for patients with liver disease”. These complement—not supersede—disease-specific evidence.
- **9.** **ANZCA anaesthesia training program curriculum (December 2025, v1.14).** [ANZCA curriculum](https://www.anzca.edu.au/education-training/anaesthesia-training-program/anaesthesia-training-program-curriculum). The complete parent LO wording and codes are in the workbook and curriculum; the Set 5 crosswalk above maps only the components assigned to this set.

Scope and date note: compiled November 2026 for ANZCA Final examination learning. Pharmacology, guideline doses, trial interpretation and local protocols should be rechecked when used in clinical care or final pre-exam revision.
